Mrs. Nawal, 61, has had short spinning attacks for two weeks, each lasting less than a minute. They happen when she turns over in bed or looks up to hang the washing. She has no hearing loss, ringing, headache or weakness.

Dr. Ihab did a test where he turned her head to the right and laid her back quickly. Her eyes flickered in a twisting pattern for twenty seconds and she felt dizzy. Her neurological exam was normal.

He explained that this was benign positional vertigo, caused by small crystals in the inner ear. He told her it was not dangerous and that it often settles.

He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months. He did not try any head movements to treat it, saying "the tablets will settle it".
h: He prescribed betahistine and prochlorperazine to take every day for three months

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave long-term tablets for positional vertigo and did not treat it with a head maneuver.
a.x: Mrs. Nawal should have had the Epley maneuver in clinic, which moves the crystals back.
a.w: BPPV is treated with the Epley maneuver. Long-term sedating tablets slow recovery and raise the risk of falls in older people.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told her it was not dangerous.
a.x: He should have warned her it might be a stroke.
a.w: Short positional spinning with a normal exam and a positive test is BPPV, which is harmless.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a test that made her dizzy.
a.x: The test was cruel.
a.w: The Dix-Hallpike test confirms BPPV.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her nervous system.
a.x: That was unnecessary.
a.w: A normal neurological exam helps rule out a stroke.

s:
Fares, 3, was brought in by his mother because he had pushed a bead up his right nostril an hour ago. He was breathing fine and playing. There was no bleeding. Mrs. Laila had tried to pull it out with tweezers at home but could not reach it.

Dr. Omar looked in Fares's nose with a light and saw a round, shiny bead just inside the right nostril. Fares was calm on his mother's lap.

Dr. Omar explained to the mother that he would try to get the bead out. He asked her to cover her mouth over Fares's mouth and blow gently while blocking the other nostril, "the mother's kiss". When this didn't work, he tried to grab the bead with long tweezers.

The smooth bead slipped back further. Dr. Omar kept trying with the tweezers four more times while Fares cried and struggled. He wrote "foreign body in situ, try again tomorrow".
h: Dr. Omar kept trying with the tweezers four more times while Fares cried and struggled

a.o: Dr. Omar kept trying to grab a smooth bead with tweezers, pushing it further back while the child struggled.
a.x: After the first failed attempt, Fares should have been referred to ENT for removal with the right tools.
a.w: Round objects slip from tweezers and can be pushed back into the airway. Repeated tries on a struggling child are unsafe.

a.o: Dr. Omar tried the "mother's kiss".
a.x: That was unsafe.
a.w: The mother's kiss is a safe first try for nasal foreign bodies.

a.o: Dr. Omar looked with a light.
a.x: A scan was needed.
a.w: Looking with a light is enough to see a bead near the nostril.

a.o: Dr. Omar let Fares sit on his mother's lap.
a.x: Fares should have been held flat.
a.w: A calm child on a parent's lap is easier to examine.

s:
Hana, 22, had her tonsils removed eight days ago. She came in after spitting out a small amount of fresh blood twice in the evening. She had been eating normally and taking ibuprofen and paracetamol for the pain.

Dr. Mohamed found a small clot on the left tonsil bed. Her pulse was 96 and her blood pressure normal. Her blood count was normal. The bleeding had stopped.

He told her that some bleeding is common around day seven to ten after the operation, as the scabs come off. He asked her to gargle with cold water.

As she looked well and the bleeding had stopped, he sent her home and told her to come back if it bled again. He did not call ENT or keep her for observation.
h: he sent her home and told her to come back if it bled again

a.o: Dr. Mohamed sent home a woman who had bled from her tonsil bed instead of keeping her for observation.
a.x: Hana should have been admitted under ENT for observation and treatment, even though it had stopped.
a.w: A small bleed after tonsillectomy can come before a big one. Patients are kept in hospital to watch.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed said bleeding is common at day seven to ten.
a.x: Bleeding after a week is never normal.
a.w: Secondary bleeding is most common between days five and ten.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed checked her blood count.
a.x: The blood count was unnecessary.
a.w: A blood count helps judge how much she had lost.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed told her to gargle cold water.
a.x: Gargling was dangerous.
a.w: Cold water can help small vessels close.

t: Hearing aid for a blocked ear
s:
Mr. Fouad, 74, came to clinic with his wife, who said he turned the television up too loud and kept asking her to repeat herself. He felt he could hear well in quiet rooms but not in busy places. He has worked in a factory for forty years.

Dr. Hala looked in both ears and found both canals completely blocked with hard wax. She could not see either eardrum.

She explained that hearing often gets worse with age and noise. She asked about dizziness and ringing, which he did not have.

She sent him for a hearing test and fitting of hearing aids, writing "age-related hearing loss". She did not treat the wax first.
h: She sent him for a hearing test and fitting of hearing aids, writing "age-related hearing loss". She did not treat the wax first

a.o: Dr. Hala sent Mr. Fouad for hearing aids without clearing the wax that blocked both ears.
a.x: The wax should have been removed first, with a hearing test afterwards.
a.w: Wax blocking the canals can cause a big hearing loss. Hearing tests and aid fittings are not accurate until it is cleared.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked about dizziness and ringing.
a.x: That was not relevant.
a.w: Dizziness or ringing may point to other ear problems.

a.o: Dr. Hala said hearing often gets worse with age and noise.
a.x: She should have said nothing.
a.w: Age and noise are common causes of hearing loss.

a.o: Dr. Hala talked to his wife.
a.x: She should have spoken only to Mr. Fouad.
a.w: His wife gave useful information about his hearing at home, with him present.

s:
Mrs. Basma, 44, woke up yesterday with the right side of her face drooping. She could not close her right eye properly, her mouth drooped and her food collected in her right cheek. Sounds were loud in her right ear. She had pain behind the ear the day before.

Dr. Mahmoud found weakness of the whole right face, including the forehead. Her ears looked normal with no blisters. Her arms and legs were normal. Her blood sugar and blood pressure were normal.

He explained that this was Bell's palsy, a nerve problem that usually gets better on its own. He prescribed prednisolone for ten days, starting today.

He told her it would probably recover in a few weeks to months. He did not give any eye drops or advice about her eye, which kept watering, "since it will recover".
h: He did not give any eye drops or advice about her eye

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud did not protect Mrs. Basma's eye, which could not close.
a.x: She should have been given lubricating eye drops by day, ointment at night and told to tape the eye shut while sleeping.
a.w: An eye that can't close dries out and can be scratched, leading to ulcers and loss of sight.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud gave steroids within 72 hours.
a.x: Steroids don't help Bell's palsy.
a.w: Steroids started within 72 hours improve recovery.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her ears for blisters.
a.x: Ears are not linked to the face.
a.w: Blisters in the ear would suggest shingles of the facial nerve, which needs antivirals.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud checked her arms and legs.
a.x: That was unnecessary.
a.w: A normal limb exam helps rule out a stroke.

t: Child with glue ear and speech delay
s:
Mostafa, 4, came in with his parents because his nursery said his speech was behind. He often said "what?" and sat close to the TV. He had several ear infections last winter. He snores at night.

Dr. Ayman found dull, retracted eardrums on both sides with a fluid level. A hearing test showed a moderate loss in both ears. His tonsils were large.

He explained that this was glue ear, fluid behind the eardrums, common after colds. He said it often clears on its own and suggested waiting three months.

He then repeated the hearing test after three months, which still showed a moderate loss. He told them it would clear by itself eventually and booked another check in a year, with no other plan.
h: booked another check in a year, with no other plan

a.o: Dr. Ayman left glue ear with lasting hearing loss and speech delay for another year.
a.x: Mostafa should have been offered grommets or hearing aids after the three-month wait.
a.w: Glue ear that lasts three months with hearing loss and speech delay needs treatment, because hearing affects speech and learning.

a.o: Dr. Ayman suggested waiting three months first.
a.x: He should have operated at once.
a.w: Most glue ear clears within three months.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a hearing test.
a.x: A hearing test was not needed.
a.w: A hearing test shows how much the fluid affects hearing.

a.o: Dr. Ayman explained glue ear is common.
a.x: He should have said it is rare.
a.w: Glue ear is very common in young children.

t: Sinusitis given antibiotics at day two
s:
Mrs. Inas, 36, came in with a blocked nose, a pressure feeling over her cheeks and a clear runny nose for two days. She had a slight temperature and a sore throat. She was otherwise healthy. She was worried because she was travelling for work next week.

Dr. Hossam found mild tenderness over her cheeks and a red nasal lining. Her temperature was 37.6°C. Her throat was a little red and her chest clear.

He explained that most sinus infections are caused by viruses and clear up in ten days. He advised saline nose rinses, a steroid nasal spray and painkillers.

Because she was travelling, he also prescribed co-amoxiclav for a week. He told her to come back if she was not better in ten days.
h: Because she was travelling, he also prescribed co-amoxiclav for a week

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave antibiotics for two days of sinus symptoms.
a.x: Mrs. Inas should have been managed without antibiotics unless symptoms lasted over ten days or got much worse.
a.w: Early sinusitis is almost always viral. Antibiotics don't help and cause side effects.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised a steroid nasal spray.
a.x: Steroids are dangerous in infection.
a.w: Steroid nasal sprays ease swelling in sinusitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised saline rinses.
a.x: Rinses don't help.
a.w: Saline rinses clear mucus and ease symptoms.

a.o: Dr. Hossam said most sinus infections clear in ten days.
a.x: They usually last a month.
a.w: Viral sinusitis usually improves within ten days.

s:
Mohamed, 19, was punched in the face during a football match. His nose bled for ten minutes and then stopped. He came in two hours later. His nose was swollen and bent to the left. He was breathing through both sides.

Dr. Eman checked inside his nose with a light and saw a purple swelling on the middle wall that blocked the left nostril. It was soft when she pressed it. He had no clear fluid from his nose and no double vision.

She explained that the nose was probably broken and that the swelling would settle. She told him to put ice on it and take paracetamol. She booked an ENT clinic visit in a week to check whether it needed straightening.

She did not mention the swelling on the middle wall of the nose and wrote "nasal fracture, ENT clinic 1 week".
h: She did not mention the swelling on the middle wall of the nose

a.o: Dr. Eman did not arrange urgent drainage of a blood collection on the nasal septum.
a.x: Mohamed should have been seen by ENT the same day to drain the septal hematoma.
a.w: A septal hematoma can cut off blood to the cartilage, leading to an abscess and a collapsed nose within days.

a.o: Dr. Eman booked ENT clinic in a week for the broken nose.
a.x: The nose should have been straightened that day.
a.w: Swelling must settle before a broken nose is judged; five to ten days is usual.

a.o: Dr. Eman checked for clear fluid from his nose.
a.x: That was not needed.
a.w: Clear fluid could mean a skull base fracture.

a.o: Dr. Eman advised ice.
a.x: Heat is better.
a.w: Ice reduces swelling.

t: One-sided nasal blockage in an adult
s:
Mr. Hesham, 56, a carpenter, came in with a blocked left nostril for four months. He sometimes had blood-stained mucus from that side and a reduced sense of smell. He had lost some weight. He has worked with hardwood dust for thirty years.

Dr. Nesma looked inside with a light and saw a red, swollen area high in the left nostril. The right side was clear. He had no neck lumps. His eye movements were normal.

She explained that this was probably a polyp from allergy and gave him a steroid nasal spray for three months. She told him to rinse with salt water.

She booked him back in three months, and wrote "nasal polyps, trial of steroids". She did not arrange a scope or a scan.
h: She did not arrange a scope or a scan

a.o: Dr. Nesma treated one-sided nasal blockage with bleeding in a woodworker as polyps without a scope or scan.
a.x: Mr. Hesham should have been urgently referred for a nasal endoscopy and scan to rule out a tumor.
a.w: Polyps are usually on both sides. One-sided blockage with bleeding, weight loss and wood dust exposure can be a nose or sinus cancer.

a.o: Dr. Nesma asked about his work.
a.x: His job was irrelevant.
a.w: Hardwood dust is linked to nasal cancer.

a.o: Dr. Nesma checked his eye movements.
a.x: The eyes are not part of a nose exam.
a.w: Eye problems can mean a growth spreading from the sinuses.

a.o: Dr. Nesma checked for neck lumps.
a.x: Neck lumps were not relevant.
a.w: Neck lumps can be a sign of cancer spreading.

s:
Mrs. Ola, 49, came in two hours after eating fish for lunch. She felt something sharp stuck in her throat on the right side, just above her collarbone. Swallowing hurt and she could swallow her saliva only slowly. She had no breathing difficulty.

Dr. Ahmed looked in her mouth and at her tonsils with a light and saw no bone. Her neck was not swollen. Her voice was normal.

He explained that sometimes a bone scratches the throat and leaves a feeling that it is still there. He told her to eat soft bread to push it down.

He sent her home with painkillers and told her to come back if she was not better in a week. He did not arrange a scope or X-ray.
h: He did not arrange a scope or X-ray

a.o: Dr. Ahmed sent home a woman with a fish bone feeling low in her throat, pain on swallowing and trouble with saliva, without a scope.
a.x: Mrs. Ola should have had a neck X-ray and a scope by ENT to find and remove the bone.
a.w: A bone stuck low in the throat can make a hole in the gullet and cause a serious infection. Pain on swallowing and trouble with saliva suggest it is still there.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked her tonsils.
a.x: The tonsils were irrelevant.
a.w: Fish bones often stick in the tonsils.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed explained that a scratch can feel like a stuck bone.
a.x: That was misleading.
a.w: A scratch often feels like a bone; it was the low position and saliva trouble that needed checking.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave painkillers.
a.x: She should not have had painkillers.
a.w: Painkillers help her swallow.

s:
Laila, 2, woke up at night with a barking cough and a hoarse voice. She had a cold for two days. Her parents brought her in because she was making a harsh noise when breathing in, even while sitting quietly.

Dr. Tamer found her alert, with a temperature of 38°C. She had a noisy breath at rest and mild pulling in at the bottom of her neck. Her oxygen was 96 percent. She was drinking.

He explained that this was croup, a viral infection of the voice box. He told the parents to keep her calm and avoid upsetting her.

He advised them to sit in a steamy bathroom with her at home, saying "steam is the best treatment". He sent them home without any medicine.
h: He advised them to sit in a steamy bathroom with her at home, saying "steam is the best treatment"

a.o: Dr. Tamer sent home a toddler with croup and noise at rest without a dose of dexamethasone.
a.x: Laila should have had a single dose of oral dexamethasone, and been watched before going home.
a.w: Steroids reduce swelling in croup and lower the chance of needing hospital care. Steam has not been shown to help.

a.o: Dr. Tamer told them to keep her calm.
a.x: Calm doesn't matter.
a.w: Crying makes croup worse, so keeping a child calm helps.

a.o: Dr. Tamer checked her oxygen.
a.x: Oxygen checks were unnecessary.
a.w: Low oxygen is a sign of severe croup.

a.o: Dr. Tamer explained that croup is viral.
a.x: He should have said it was bacterial.
a.w: Croup is usually caused by viruses.

t: Hearing loss in a baby missed
s:
Baby Salma, 9 months old, came in for a routine check. Her mother said she smiled and played but did not turn to her name or loud noises. She did not babble like her older brother had. She was born early, at 32 weeks, and spent three weeks in the neonatal unit with an infection treated with gentamicin.

Dr. Rehab found a happy baby who was sitting and reaching for toys. Her ears looked normal.

She explained that babies develop at different speeds, especially premature babies. She told the mother to talk to Salma a lot.

She asked the mother to come back in six months to see if Salma started talking. She did not arrange a hearing test, saying "her newborn screening must have been normal". The mother wasn't sure whether the screening was done.
h: She did not arrange a hearing test, saying "her newborn screening must have been normal"

a.o: Dr. Rehab did not arrange a hearing test for a baby who doesn't react to sounds and had risk factors.
a.x: Salma should have had an urgent hearing test.
a.w: Premature babies who had gentamicin are at high risk of hearing loss. Not turning to sounds or babbling at 9 months needs testing now.

a.o: Dr. Rehab said babies develop at different speeds.
a.x: That was false reassurance.
a.w: Babies do vary, but warning signs still need checking.

a.o: Dr. Rehab told the mother to talk to Salma a lot.
a.x: Talking doesn't help.
a.w: Talking to babies supports language.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Salma's sitting and reaching.
a.x: Movement was irrelevant.
a.w: Checking all development helps see if a delay is only in hearing.

s:
Mrs. Samira, 52, had her thyroid removed this morning for a large goiter. In the evening the nurse called Dr. Kareem because she was anxious and short of breath. Her neck was swelling under the dressing and she had a high-pitched noise when breathing in.

Her oxygen was 92 percent and her pulse 118. Her voice was weak. The neck wound looked tense and swollen. She had been given a blood thinner injection for clot prevention in the afternoon.

Dr. Kareem gave oxygen and nebulized adrenaline and called the surgeon and the anesthetist. He asked for blood tests including calcium.

While waiting, he left the stitches in and the dressing on, writing "await surgeon to assess". The swelling kept growing and her breathing got noisier.
h: he left the stitches in and the dressing on, writing "await surgeon to assess"

a.o: Dr. Kareem left the stitches in a swelling neck wound with stridor after thyroid surgery.
a.x: The dressing and stitches should have been opened at once at the bedside to release the blood clot.
a.w: Bleeding under a thyroid wound can squash the windpipe within minutes. Opening the wound to let the clot out saves life.

a.o: Dr. Kareem checked her calcium.
a.x: Calcium was not relevant.
a.w: Low calcium is a common problem after thyroid surgery.

a.o: Dr. Kareem called the anesthetist.
a.x: The anesthetist was not needed.
a.w: Airway problems need an anesthetist.

a.o: Dr. Kareem gave nebulized adrenaline.
a.x: Adrenaline was useless.
a.w: It can briefly reduce swelling while help comes.

s:
Mr. Raafat, 60, came in about a white patch on the side of his tongue for four months. It did not wipe off and was not painful. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and chews tobacco. He drinks alcohol most evenings.

Dr. Inas found a 1.5 cm white patch with a slightly rough surface on the left side of his tongue. There were no neck lumps. His teeth were in poor condition.

She explained that this could be leukoplakia, a white patch that sometimes turns into cancer. She advised better dental care and booked a dentist appointment.

She told him to rinse with an antifungal mouthwash for two weeks and come back if it didn't go. She did not take a biopsy or mention stopping smoking and chewing tobacco.
h: She did not take a biopsy or mention stopping smoking and chewing tobacco

a.o: Dr. Inas did not biopsy a white tongue patch in a heavy smoker or tell him to stop tobacco.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have had a biopsy and strong advice and help to stop smoking, chewing tobacco and drinking.
a.w: Leukoplakia can be pre-cancer, especially in smokers and drinkers. A biopsy shows the risk, and stopping tobacco is the most important step.

a.o: Dr. Inas booked a dentist appointment.
a.x: Teeth were irrelevant.
a.w: Poor teeth can rub the tongue and keep it irritated.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked for neck lumps.
a.x: Neck lumps were irrelevant.
a.w: Neck lumps could mean spread of cancer.

a.o: Dr. Inas explained it might turn into cancer.
a.x: She should not have mentioned cancer.
a.w: Patients need honest information.

t: Tinnitus in one ear not scanned
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 47, came in with ringing in her left ear for six months. She also felt she heard less on the left and had slight unsteadiness. Her right ear was fine. She has no history of loud noise exposure.

Dr. Fouad found both eardrums normal. Her hearing test showed a nerve hearing loss in the left ear only. Her facial movement and feeling were normal. She works as an accountant and finds the ringing worst at night when the office is quiet. She drinks two coffees a day and takes no regular medicines.

He explained that ringing in the ears is very common and usually harmless. He suggested background noise at night and relaxation exercises.

He told her she could live with it and booked no further tests, writing "tinnitus, reassured".
h: booked no further tests, writing "tinnitus, reassured"

a.o: Dr. Fouad did not order an MRI for one-sided ringing with one-sided nerve hearing loss and unsteadiness.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had an MRI to look for a growth on the hearing nerve.
a.w: Ringing and hearing loss in one ear can be caused by an acoustic neuroma. It needs an MRI.

a.o: Dr. Fouad suggested background noise at night.
a.x: That makes tinnitus worse.
a.w: Background sound can help mask the ringing.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked her facial movement.
a.x: The face is not related.
a.w: A growth on the nerve can press on the facial nerve.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did a hearing test.
a.x: The hearing test was pointless.
a.w: It showed the one-sided loss, which is important.

t: Steroid drops for a perforated ear
s:
Ahmed, 11, came in with a smelly yellow discharge from his left ear for ten days. He had a bad ear infection a month ago that hurt a lot and then suddenly felt better when the ear started running. He had no fever now and no pain. His hearing on the left felt dull.

Dr. Samah cleaned the canal gently with a small cotton wick under a light and saw a small hole in the eardrum with mucus coming through. The skin behind the ear was normal and not tender. His facial movements were normal.

She explained that the infection had made a small hole in the eardrum, which usually heals by itself. She told him to keep the ear dry in the shower with cotton wool and Vaseline and to avoid swimming for now.

She prescribed gentamicin ear drops three times a day for three weeks, "to clear it well", and booked a check in six weeks to see if the hole had healed.
h: She prescribed gentamicin ear drops three times a day for three weeks

a.o: Dr. Samah gave long-term gentamicin drops into an ear with a hole in the eardrum.
a.x: Ahmed should have had ciprofloxacin drops, which do not harm the inner ear, for about a week.
a.w: Gentamicin can pass through a hole in the eardrum and damage hearing and balance. Quinolone drops are used for perforations.

a.o: Dr. Samah told him to avoid swimming.
a.x: Swimming is fine.
a.w: Water in a perforated ear can cause infection.

a.o: Dr. Samah said the hole usually heals by itself.
a.x: Holes always need surgery.
a.w: Most small perforations after infection heal within weeks.

a.o: Dr. Samah cleaned the canal gently.
a.x: The canal should not be touched.
a.w: Gentle cleaning lets drops reach the infection.

s:
Mr. Hamed, 72, has had type 2 diabetes for fifteen years. He came for his diabetes review. He takes metformin 1 g twice a day and gliclazide. His HbA1c was 58 mmol/mol. He had been feeling a bit tired and his ankles swelled at the end of the day.

His blood tests showed his kidney function had fallen over the past year. His eGFR was now 24. His potassium was normal. His blood pressure was 146/88 and his urine showed protein.

Dr. Rasha praised his sugar control and advised him to keep walking. She added ramipril for his blood pressure and his kidneys and asked for repeat kidney tests in two weeks.

He lives with his wife, who cooks low-sugar meals for him. He also takes amlodipine and aspirin. He had noticed passing urine more at night. His feet were checked and were healthy. He said he would rather not start injections and asked whether his kidneys could get better.

She told him to carry on with both his diabetes tablets at the same doses because his sugar was well controlled, and booked his next review in six months.
h: She told him to carry on with both his diabetes tablets at the same doses

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mr. Hamed on full-dose metformin with an eGFR of 24.
a.x: His metformin should have been stopped and his diabetes treatment changed, for example to a DPP-4 inhibitor or insulin.
a.w: Metformin builds up when the kidneys fail and can cause lactic acidosis. It should be stopped when eGFR is below 30.

a.o: Dr. Rasha added ramipril for a man with weak kidneys.
a.x: Ramipril harms the kidneys.
a.w: ACE inhibitors protect the kidneys in diabetes with protein in the urine, with kidney tests checked after starting.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for kidney tests in two weeks.
a.x: Tests could wait for six months.
a.w: Kidney tests are needed soon after starting ramipril.

a.o: Dr. Rasha advised him to keep walking.
a.x: Walking strains the heart.
a.w: Exercise is good for diabetes.

t: Sliding scale insulin in a type 1
s:
Nada, 20, has type 1 diabetes and was admitted with appendicitis. She had her appendix removed this morning and was allowed to drink but not eat yet. She usually takes glargine at night and rapid insulin with meals.

Her sugar was 9 mmol/L before surgery. In the evening the nurse said her sugar was 12. Dr. Basel checked her ketones, which were low. She was alert and in mild pain.

He wrote her up for IV fluids, painkillers and anti-sickness medicine.

Nada has had diabetes since she was nine and usually manages it herself with a pump-like routine of carb counting. She had felt sick before surgery and was worried about her sugars. Her mother, a pharmacist, asked whether her night insulin would still be given. Her pain was controlled with paracetamol and a little morphine.

Because she was not eating, he stopped all her usual insulin, including the glargine, and wrote "sliding scale rapid insulin if sugar over 14". He asked for sugar checks every four hours.
h: he stopped all her usual insulin, including the glargine

a.o: Dr. Basel stopped all of Nada's background insulin because she was not eating.
a.x: Nada should have continued her glargine and been put on a variable rate insulin infusion with glucose until eating.
a.w: People with type 1 diabetes always need background insulin. Without it, they can develop diabetic ketoacidosis within hours.

a.o: Dr. Basel checked her ketones.
a.x: Ketones were not needed.
a.w: Ketones show whether she is going into DKA.

a.o: Dr. Basel gave IV fluids.
a.x: She should have had nothing.
a.w: Fluids keep her hydrated while not eating.

a.o: Dr. Basel asked for sugar checks every four hours.
a.x: Sugar checks were too frequent.
a.w: Regular checks are needed around surgery.

s:
Mrs. Somaya, 45, has an underactive thyroid and takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms every morning. Her TSH had been normal for years. Six months ago she started ferrous sulphate for heavy periods. Now she feels tired, cold and has put on 3 kg.

Her TSH was 9.2 mU/L, raised. Her ferritin had improved. She said she takes all her tablets together with breakfast and tea to remember them.

Dr. Hany checked her pulse and skin. He asked about her periods, which were lighter now.

She works as a bank clerk and leaves home at seven, so she swallows everything in one go with her breakfast tea and a slice of bread with cheese. Her periods had become lighter on tranexamic acid. Her hair felt dry, and her colleagues had joked that she was always wearing a cardigan in summer.

He increased her levothyroxine to 150 micrograms and booked a TSH check in six weeks. He did not comment on how she takes her tablets.
h: He did not comment on how she takes her tablets

a.o: Dr. Hany increased the levothyroxine dose without telling Mrs. Somaya to take it apart from her iron and food.
a.x: She should have been told to take levothyroxine on an empty stomach and at least four hours apart from iron.
a.w: Iron and food stop levothyroxine being absorbed. Separating them may be all she needs.

a.o: Dr. Hany booked a TSH check in six weeks.
a.x: TSH should be checked in a week.
a.w: TSH takes about six weeks to settle after a dose change.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked about her periods.
a.x: Periods have nothing to do with thyroid.
a.w: Heavy periods caused her low iron and are linked to thyroid problems.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked her pulse.
a.x: The pulse was irrelevant.
a.w: A slow pulse is a sign of an underactive thyroid.

s:
Mr. Hussein, 48, was admitted vomiting, very weak and dizzy. He has had tiredness and weight loss for months and his skin had darkened, especially in the creases of his hands. His blood pressure was 84/50 and his pulse 118.

His sodium was 124 mmol/L, potassium 6.1 and his sugar 3.4. He had no fever. Dr. Rania gave him IV saline and dextrose.

She sent a random cortisol and ACTH level. She explained that his adrenal glands might not be making enough hormones and that the test results would come back in two days.

His wife said he had craved salty crisps for weeks and had fainted once at the mosque. He had lost 8 kg in three months. He had no fever, cough or diarrhea, and he takes no medicines. Dr. Rania noticed dark patches on his gums and the old scar on his knee looked darker than the skin around it.

She wrote "await cortisol result before steroids, to avoid affecting the test". His blood pressure was still low after the fluids.
h: await cortisol result before steroids, to avoid affecting the test

a.o: Dr. Rania waited for the cortisol result before giving steroids to a man in adrenal crisis.
a.x: Mr. Hussein should have had IV hydrocortisone at once, after the blood sample was taken.
a.w: Adrenal crisis is deadly. The blood sample can be taken first, but steroid treatment must not wait for the result.

a.o: Dr. Rania gave dextrose.
a.x: Sugar was not needed.
a.w: His sugar was low, so dextrose was right.

a.o: Dr. Rania sent an ACTH level.
a.x: ACTH is not useful.
a.w: ACTH helps find whether the problem is in the adrenals or the pituitary.

a.o: Dr. Rania gave saline.
a.x: Saline will make his sodium worse.
a.w: He was dry and low on sodium, so saline is right.

s:
Mrs. Heba, 33, has Graves' disease and stopped her carbimazole three weeks ago. She came in with a high fever of 40°C, a racing heart at 150 and confusion. She had a chest infection for three days. She was sweating, shaking and had diarrhea.

Her ECG showed fast atrial fibrillation. Her thyroid tests showed very high T4. Her blood pressure was 104/60.

Dr. Ahmed started IV fluids, propranolol and high-dose carbimazole, then Lugol's iodine an hour later. He started hydrocortisone and IV antibiotics for her chest.

Her husband said she had stopped the tablets because she felt well and was planning a pregnancy. She weighed 52 kg and had lost 4 kg in the last month. Her eyes were staring and her hands shook. Her chest X-ray showed a patch on the right. She had no allergies.

For her fever, he gave her 900 mg of aspirin and asked the nurses to sponge her down. He asked ICU to see her.
h: For her fever, he gave her 900 mg of aspirin

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave aspirin for fever in thyroid storm.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had paracetamol and cooling for her fever.
a.w: Aspirin frees thyroid hormone from proteins in the blood and makes thyroid storm worse.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave iodine an hour after carbimazole.
a.x: Iodine should come first.
a.w: Iodine is given at least an hour after carbimazole so the thyroid can't use it to make more hormone.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave hydrocortisone.
a.x: Steroids are not needed.
a.w: Steroids block hormone conversion and support the adrenals in thyroid storm.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed gave propranolol.
a.x: Beta blockers are dangerous.
a.w: Propranolol controls the heart rate and symptoms.

s:
Mr. Fathy, 54, a bus driver, has type 2 diabetes and started insulin six months ago. He came for a review. His HbA1c was 49 mmol/mol, much better than before. He said he had a few shaky, sweaty spells at work in the late morning, which went away when he ate a biscuit.

His blood sugar diary showed readings as low as 3.2 mmol/L twice last month. He checks his sugar only at breakfast.

Dr. Sherine praised his control. She reduced his morning insulin a little and asked him to check his sugar before meals.

He drives the 6 a.m. school route and often skips breakfast, eating a sandwich at the depot around eleven. He has never had a crash or a near miss. He also takes metformin and atorvastatin. His wife had noticed he was grumpy and sweaty some mornings and had started packing dates in his bag.

She told him that low sugars are common when starting insulin and that he could keep driving his bus as usual. She did not discuss the driving rules.
h: he could keep driving his bus as usual

a.o: Dr. Sherine told a bus driver on insulin having low sugars that he could keep driving as usual.
a.x: Mr. Fathy should have been told to stop driving his bus, inform the licensing authority and check his sugar before and every two hours while driving.
a.w: Low sugars while driving a bus could kill. Insulin users who drive professionally must follow strict rules.

a.o: Dr. Sherine reduced his morning insulin.
a.x: She should have increased it.
a.w: His sugar was going too low, so a smaller dose was right.

a.o: Dr. Sherine praised his HbA1c.
a.x: His HbA1c was too high.
a.w: 49 mmol/mol is a good result.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked him to check his sugar before meals.
a.x: Checking once a day is enough.
a.w: More checks help find when sugars go low.

s:
Mrs. Zeinab, 74, was admitted confused after a week of vomiting. She takes a thiazide water tablet for blood pressure. Her sodium was 112 mmol/L. She had no seizures and was talking, though muddled.

Dr. Mohamed stopped her thiazide and started 0.9 percent saline. He checked her urine sodium and osmolality.

After 24 hours, her sodium was 128. She was more alert and eating. The nurses were pleased.

She lives alone and her son found her in bed, unable to say what day it was. She had been drinking lots of tea because she felt thirsty. She also takes amlodipine and an antidepressant, sertraline, which she started two months ago. Her blood pressure was 104/60 and her mouth was dry.

Dr. Mohamed wrote "excellent improvement, continue saline at the same rate" and booked the next sodium for the following morning.
h: wrote "excellent improvement, continue saline at the same rate"

a.o: Dr. Mohamed let Mrs. Zeinab's sodium rise by 16 in a day and kept the saline going.
a.x: Her sodium should have risen no more than 8 to 10 in 24 hours, with fluids slowed and sodium checked every few hours.
a.w: Correcting long-standing low sodium too fast can damage the brain (osmotic demyelination), causing paralysis.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed stopped her thiazide.
a.x: The thiazide should continue.
a.w: Thiazides cause low sodium, so stopping is right.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed gave saline.
a.x: She should have had water restriction only.
a.w: After vomiting she was dry, and saline helps.

a.o: Dr. Mohamed checked her urine.
a.x: Urine was irrelevant.
a.w: Urine tests help find the cause of low sodium.

s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 29, has a small prolactinoma, 7 mm on MRI, found when her periods stopped. She takes cabergoline and her periods came back. She now found she was pregnant at five weeks and was overjoyed.

She had no headaches or vision problems. Her visual fields were normal.

Dr. Ihab explained that small prolactinomas rarely cause problems in pregnancy. He told her to stop cabergoline now that she was pregnant.

She had tried for a baby for two years before the tumor was found. Her husband came with her and asked many questions. She said she felt sick in the mornings and her breasts were tender. Her last prolactin, before the pregnancy, was normal on treatment. She works as a graphic designer and spends hours at a screen.

He booked an MRI of her pituitary every month during pregnancy "to make sure it doesn't grow" and asked for prolactin levels every month.
h: He booked an MRI of her pituitary every month during pregnancy

a.o: Dr. Ihab booked monthly pituitary MRIs during pregnancy for a small prolactinoma with no symptoms.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have been monitored by asking about headaches and vision, with visual field tests if symptoms appeared.
a.w: Small prolactinomas rarely grow in pregnancy. Routine MRIs are not needed; scans are done only if symptoms appear.

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped cabergoline in pregnancy.
a.x: Cabergoline should continue.
a.w: Most women with small prolactinomas stop the drug in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Ihab said small prolactinomas rarely cause problems.
a.x: That was false reassurance.
a.w: The risk of growth is small in microadenomas.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked her visual fields.
a.x: Vision was not relevant.
a.w: A growing pituitary tumor can press on the nerves of sight.

t: HbA1c target for a frail older woman
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 86, has type 2 diabetes and dementia. She lives in a care home. She takes gliclazide and metformin. Her HbA1c was 54 mmol/mol. The care home said she had two falls in a month, both in the morning, and was sometimes sweaty and confused before breakfast.

Her finger-prick sugars before breakfast were as low as 3.1.

Dr. Gamal checked her feet and blood pressure, which were fine. He asked for her kidney tests, which were stable.

Her daughter visits on Fridays and said her mother had been eating less since a chest infection in the winter. Mrs. Hanem needs help to walk and uses a frame. She takes eight other tablets a day, including a water tablet. Her weight had dropped by 4 kg in six months, and her blood pressure was 128/70.

He wrote "HbA1c above target of 48; increase gliclazide to tighten control" and asked the care home to keep checking her sugars.
h: increase gliclazide to tighten control

a.o: Dr. Gamal increased gliclazide in a frail woman with dementia who was falling and having low sugars.
a.x: Her gliclazide should have been reduced or stopped, with a relaxed HbA1c target.
a.w: In frail older people, low sugars cause falls and confusion. Targets are relaxed to avoid them.

a.o: Dr. Gamal checked her feet.
a.x: Feet are not important at her age.
a.w: Foot checks prevent ulcers at any age.

a.o: Dr. Gamal asked for kidney tests.
a.x: Kidney tests were not needed.
a.w: Metformin and gliclazide depend on kidney function.

a.o: Dr. Gamal asked the care home to keep checking sugars.
a.x: Checks are pointless.
a.w: Checks find low sugars.

s:
Mrs. Nabila, 66, has breast cancer that has spread to her bones. She came in confused, thirsty and constipated. She had been vomiting for two days. Her calcium was 3.6 mmol/L and her kidney function was worse than usual.

She looked dry, with a dry tongue and low blood pressure of 98/60.

Dr. Samir gave her 40 mg of IV furosemide straight away to "flush out the calcium". He then planned to start IV saline later.

Her daughter said she had been very thirsty for a week and passing urine all the time. Mrs. Nabila takes letrozole and had a bone-strengthening infusion six months ago. She has bone pain in her back and hips, and takes regular paracetamol and a little morphine. Her heart sounded normal and her chest was clear.

He asked the oncology team to see her and planned a bisphosphonate infusion. He gave her a laxative for the constipation.
h: gave her 40 mg of IV furosemide straight away to "flush out the calcium"

a.o: Dr. Samir gave furosemide to a dry woman with high calcium before giving fluids.
a.x: Mrs. Nabila should have had plenty of IV saline first, then a bisphosphonate.
a.w: Most patients with high calcium are very dry. Furosemide makes dehydration worse and can raise calcium. Fluids come first.

a.o: Dr. Samir planned a bisphosphonate.
a.x: Bisphosphonates are not used for calcium.
a.w: IV bisphosphonates lower calcium from bone cancer.

a.o: Dr. Samir gave a laxative.
a.x: Laxatives are unsafe.
a.w: High calcium causes constipation, so laxatives help.

a.o: Dr. Samir called the oncology team.
a.x: Oncology was not needed.
a.w: Her cancer team should be involved.

s:
Mr. Amr, 52, has had severe asthma and has taken prednisolone 15 mg daily for a year. He came to the clinic for a check. His asthma was better but he had put on weight.

Dr. Mona checked his blood pressure and sugar, which were slightly raised. She arranged a bone scan.

She explained the side effects of long-term steroids and said they would try to reduce the dose slowly.

He works as a long-distance lorry driver and is often away from home for days. He said he sometimes forgets his evening tablets. He had a bad chest infection last winter, when he could not keep food down for two days. He also takes a calcium and vitamin D tablet and an inhaler.

She did not give him a steroid card or tell him what to do if he became unwell or vomited. She booked a review in three months.
h: She did not give him a steroid card or tell him what to do if he became unwell or vomited

a.o: Dr. Mona did not give a steroid card or sick day rules to a man on long-term prednisolone.
a.x: Mr. Amr should have been given a steroid card and told to double his dose when ill and seek help if vomiting.
a.w: Long-term steroids stop the body making its own. Illness or vomiting can cause an adrenal crisis.

a.o: Dr. Mona arranged a bone scan.
a.x: A bone scan was unnecessary.
a.w: Long-term steroids thin bones.

a.o: Dr. Mona checked his sugar.
a.x: Sugar was irrelevant.
a.w: Steroids raise blood sugar.

a.o: Dr. Mona planned to reduce the dose slowly.
a.x: Steroids should stop at once.
a.w: Stopping suddenly can cause adrenal crisis.

s:
Mrs. Raghda, 38, noticed a lump in the front of her neck. It moved when she swallowed. She had no voice change or trouble swallowing. Her thyroid tests were normal.

An ultrasound showed a 2.2 cm solid nodule with tiny spots of calcium and irregular edges. No neck lymph nodes were swollen.

Dr. Waleed explained that most thyroid nodules are harmless. He told her many women have them.

She works as a teacher and has two children. Her mother had a goiter. She had no history of radiation to her neck. She had felt the lump while putting on a necklace and was worried. Dr. Waleed felt the nodule, which was firm, and her voice was clear. Her calcium was normal.

He booked a repeat ultrasound in a year to see if it changed and did not arrange a needle biopsy.
h: booked a repeat ultrasound in a year to see if it changed and did not arrange a needle biopsy

a.o: Dr. Waleed planned to watch a suspicious thyroid nodule for a year without a biopsy.
a.x: Mrs. Raghda should have had a fine needle biopsy of the nodule.
a.w: A solid nodule over 1 cm with microcalcifications and irregular edges may be cancer and needs a biopsy.

a.o: Dr. Waleed said most nodules are harmless.
a.x: He should not reassure.
a.w: Most thyroid nodules are benign; the ultrasound features decide what to do next.

a.o: Dr. Waleed checked her thyroid tests.
a.x: Thyroid tests are pointless.
a.w: Thyroid function is checked in all nodules.

a.o: Dr. Waleed checked for neck nodes.
a.x: Lymph nodes are not related.
a.w: Swollen nodes could mean thyroid cancer.

t: Pheochromocytoma given a beta blocker first
s:
Mr. Raafat, 41, came in with a blood pressure of 220/120, a pounding headache, sweating and palpitations. He has had similar attacks for months. His urine tests showed very high metanephrines and a CT showed a 4 cm mass on his left adrenal gland.

Dr. Nihal diagnosed a pheochromocytoma and asked the surgeons to plan an operation.

For his fast heart, she started propranolol 40 mg three times a day. She planned to add phenoxybenzamine in a few days.

He is a gym coach and had been told by his GP that his attacks were panic attacks. He had lost weight and his sugar was mildly raised. His father died suddenly in his forties. His heart rate was 118 and his blood pressure dropped when he stood up.

She asked for a heart echo and told him the operation would cure him.
h: she started propranolol 40 mg three times a day. She planned to add phenoxybenzamine in a few days

a.o: Dr. Nihal started a beta blocker before an alpha blocker in a man with a pheochromocytoma.
a.x: Mr. Raafat should have started phenoxybenzamine first, with a beta blocker added only after full alpha blockade.
a.w: Beta blockers alone leave the alpha effects of adrenaline unopposed, which can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Nihal asked for an echo.
a.x: An echo was unnecessary.
a.w: High adrenaline can damage the heart.

a.o: Dr. Nihal said the operation would cure him.
a.x: Surgery never cures it.
a.w: Removing the tumor usually cures the high blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Nihal asked the surgeons to plan an operation.
a.x: Surgery is too risky.
a.w: Surgery is the treatment.

s:
Mrs. Shaimaa, 31, had diabetes in pregnancy, treated with metformin and diet. She gave birth to a healthy baby boy three months ago and stopped metformin. She came in for her baby's vaccinations.

Dr. Tamer asked how she was. She said she was tired but happy. She had put on some weight.

He congratulated her and gave her advice about healthy eating and exercise. He encouraged her to keep breastfeeding for as long as she could. He asked about her mood, which was fine.

She had a big baby, 4.1 kg, delivered by caesarean. Her mother and two aunts have type 2 diabetes. Her BMI was 31 before pregnancy. She asked whether she could take the pill again and whether her next pregnancy would be the same. She said she had no time to exercise with a new baby.

He told her that her diabetes was "gone now" and that she did not need any more tests.
h: He told her that her diabetes was "gone now" and that she did not need any more tests

a.o: Dr. Tamer told Mrs. Shaimaa her diabetes was gone and that she needed no more tests.
a.x: She should have had a fasting sugar or HbA1c after birth and then every year.
a.w: Women who had diabetes in pregnancy have a high risk of type 2 diabetes later. Yearly checks are needed.

a.o: Dr. Tamer asked about her mood.
a.x: Mood was not relevant.
a.w: Depression after birth is common.

a.o: Dr. Tamer gave advice on healthy eating.
a.x: Diet doesn't matter now.
a.w: Healthy eating lowers her diabetes risk.

a.o: Dr. Tamer encouraged her to keep breastfeeding after diabetes in pregnancy.
a.x: She should have switched the baby to formula.
a.w: Breastfeeding is good for the baby and lowers the mother's own risk of type 2 diabetes later.

s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 68, broke her wrist after a fall on a wet floor. A bone scan showed osteoporosis. She is housebound and rarely goes outside. Her blood tests showed a vitamin D of 18 nmol/L and a calcium at the low end of normal.

Dr. Nermine explained that her bones were thin and gave her advice about preventing falls.

She started alendronic acid once a week and told her to take it on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, sitting up for half an hour.

She lives with her daughter's family and spends most days indoors watching television. She wears long clothes and a headscarf when she does go out. She has mild kidney disease and takes omeprazole for indigestion. Her wrist was set in plaster in the ER. Her teeth were in good condition.

She did not prescribe calcium or vitamin D, writing "alendronate alone is enough".
h: She did not prescribe calcium or vitamin D, writing "alendronate alone is enough"

a.o: Dr. Nermine started alendronic acid in a woman with very low vitamin D without replacing vitamin D.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had her vitamin D replaced before or with alendronate, plus calcium if her diet was low.
a.w: Bisphosphonates can drop calcium dangerously if vitamin D is low. Vitamin D is needed for the treatment to work.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told her to stay upright for half an hour.
a.x: Lying down is fine.
a.w: Staying upright stops the tablet burning her gullet.

a.o: Dr. Nermine gave advice about falls.
a.x: Falls are not related to bones.
a.w: Preventing falls lowers the chance of fractures.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told her to take it on an empty stomach.
a.x: It should be taken with food.
a.w: Food stops it being absorbed.

s:
Mr. Sabry, 63, has had type 2 diabetes for twenty years. He came in for a review. His HbA1c was 64 mmol/mol. He smokes ten cigarettes a day.

He mentioned that his feet felt numb and he had burnt his toe on a hot water bottle last month without feeling it. He had not looked at his feet.

Dr. Ayman increased his medicines and gave him advice about smoking. He checked his eyes' screening result.

He works as a farmer and is on his feet most of the day. His blood pressure was 148/90. He mentioned his eyes were fine and his last eye screening was clear. He said he sometimes walks barefoot in the house. His kidney tests were normal, and he was keen to finish quickly to get back to the fields.

He did not examine his feet because Mr. Sabry was wearing boots and "time was short". He booked a review in a year.
h: He did not examine his feet because Mr. Sabry was wearing boots and "time was short"

a.o: Dr. Ayman did not look at the feet of a diabetic man with numb feet who had burnt his toe.
a.x: Mr. Sabry's feet should have been examined, and he should have been referred to the foot team.
a.w: Numb feet and an unnoticed burn mean a high risk of ulcers and amputation. Feet must be checked.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave advice about smoking.
a.x: That wasn't relevant to diabetes.
a.w: Smoking worsens blood flow and diabetic complications.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked his eye screening.
a.x: Eyes were not relevant.
a.w: Eye screening is part of diabetes care.

a.o: Dr. Ayman increased his medicines.
a.x: His HbA1c was fine.
a.w: 64 is above target.

s:
Mr. Atef, 78, was brought in by his daughter. He had been drowsy and confused for two days, drinking little, and passing a lot of urine. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin. His sugar was 48 mmol/L, his sodium 152 and his serum osmolality 360. His ketones were 0.6.

He looked very dry, with a pulse of 112 and blood pressure 100/62. His daughter said he had a urine infection last week and had been too tired to eat. His kidney function was worse than usual, and his legs were not swollen. He had no chest pain.

Dr. Hana started an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour at once to bring the sugar down quickly. She started IV saline at 100 mL an hour because "he is old".

She asked for blood tests every two hours and a urinary catheter. She gave him a blood thinner injection to prevent clots.
h: started an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour at once to bring the sugar down quickly. She started IV saline at 100 mL an hour

a.o: Dr. Hana started insulin at once and ran the saline slowly in a very dry man with HHS.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had IV saline first, a liter in the first hour, with insulin only once the sugar stopped falling with fluids alone.
a.w: In HHS, fluids alone lower the sugar. Early insulin drops the sugar and osmolality too fast and can cause brain swelling and collapse.

a.o: Dr. Hana gave a blood thinner.
a.x: Blood thinners are not needed.
a.w: HHS raises the risk of clots.

a.o: Dr. Hana asked for a catheter.
a.x: A catheter was not needed.
a.w: Urine output guides fluid replacement.

a.o: Dr. Hana checked his bloods every two hours.
a.x: Bloods every six hours were enough.
a.w: In HHS, sodium and osmolality must be checked often so they don't fall too fast.

s:
Mrs. Nesrine, 42, came in with weight gain around her middle, a round face, thin skin that bruised easily and purple stretch marks on her belly. Her blood pressure was 152/96 and her sugar was raised.

Dr. Fady asked about her medicines. She said she had been using a strong steroid cream from a pharmacy all over her body for two years to lighten her skin.

He explained that the cream was absorbed and causing her symptoms. He asked for a cortisol test.

She works in a beauty salon and said the cream was "popular with customers". She also had acne on her shoulders and her periods had become irregular. She takes no tablets. Her mood had been low and she was sleeping badly. Dr. Fady saw thin skin with fine veins on her face and arms.

He told her to stop the cream at once. He did not mention the risks of stopping suddenly.
h: He told her to stop the cream at once

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mrs. Nesrine to stop a strong steroid used all over her body for two years at once.
a.x: Her steroid should have been reduced slowly, with a test of her own adrenal function and advice about illness.
a.w: Long-term strong steroids switch off the adrenal glands. Stopping suddenly can cause an adrenal crisis.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked about her medicines.
a.x: Medicines are not related to weight gain.
a.w: Steroids are a common cause of Cushing's syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked her sugar.
a.x: Sugar is irrelevant.
a.w: Steroids raise blood sugar.

a.o: Dr. Fady explained the cream was absorbed.
a.x: Creams can't affect the body.
a.w: Strong steroid creams over large areas are absorbed.

s:
Mrs. Yasmine, 27, has Graves' disease and takes carbimazole. She just found out she is six weeks pregnant. She feels well and her thyroid levels have been normal for months.

Dr. Nada congratulated her. She asked about her symptoms and checked her pulse, which was 82.

She explained that thyroid levels need close checks in pregnancy and asked for blood tests every month. She advised folic acid every day.

She had been diagnosed two years ago after losing weight and feeling shaky. Her eyes are not affected. She takes no other medicines apart from paracetamol for headaches. She had felt very sick in the mornings. Her husband was nervous and asked whether the baby could catch the thyroid problem.

She told her to continue carbimazole at the same dose for the whole pregnancy "as it is working well".
h: She told her to continue carbimazole at the same dose for the whole pregnancy

a.o: Dr. Nada kept Mrs. Yasmine on carbimazole in the first trimester.
a.x: She should have been switched to propylthiouracil for the first trimester.
a.w: Carbimazole can cause birth defects in early pregnancy. PTU is preferred in the first three months.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked for monthly blood tests.
a.x: Tests every three months are enough.
a.w: Thyroid levels change in pregnancy and need close checks.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked her pulse.
a.x: The pulse was irrelevant.
a.w: A fast pulse can show an overactive thyroid.

a.o: Dr. Nada added folic acid on top of her thyroid tablets.
a.x: Extra tablets should be avoided in early pregnancy.
a.w: Folic acid in early pregnancy prevents spine defects in the baby.

s:
Mr. Kamal, 66, has type 2 diabetes on insulin. He was admitted for a planned hip replacement. In the morning the nurse said he was nil by mouth from midnight for surgery at 2 p.m.

His sugar at 7 a.m. was 7.8 mmol/L. He usually takes 20 units of rapid insulin with breakfast and 30 units of long-acting at night.

Dr. Ola wrote up his usual breakfast rapid insulin of 20 units "to keep his sugar controlled". She asked the nurses to check his sugar every two hours.

He walks with a stick and lives with his wife, who usually prepares his insulin. He also takes ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. His last HbA1c was 61. The anesthetist had seen him the day before and was happy for surgery. He was worried about being hungry all morning.

She also asked for his blood pressure tablets to be given with a sip of water and checked his kidney tests.
h: Dr. Ola wrote up his usual breakfast rapid insulin of 20 units "to keep his sugar controlled"

a.o: Dr. Ola gave Mr. Kamal his full meal-time insulin while he was not eating.
a.x: His meal-time insulin should have been held while nil by mouth, with sugar checks and an insulin infusion if needed.
a.w: Rapid insulin without food causes dangerous low sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ola gave his blood pressure tablets with water.
a.x: All tablets must stop before surgery.
a.w: Most blood pressure tablets are given with a sip of water.

a.o: Dr. Ola asked for two-hourly sugar checks.
a.x: Checks are too frequent.
a.w: Frequent checks are needed while fasting.

a.o: Dr. Ola checked his kidney tests.
a.x: Kidneys don't matter.
a.w: Kidney function affects drugs and surgery.

s:
Rawan, 19, was diagnosed with diabetes at 17 and has been on insulin injections four times a day. Her mother, grandfather and uncle all have diabetes diagnosed before 25, and none of them needed insulin. Rawan is slim and has never had ketoacidosis.

Her HbA1c was 53 mmol/mol. Her antibody tests for type 1 diabetes, done last year, were negative. Her C-peptide was normal two years after diagnosis.

Dr. Hossam praised her control and adjusted her insulin. He advised carbohydrate counting.

She is studying medicine and keeps careful records. She sometimes forgets a lunchtime injection on long days at the hospital, and her sugars stay steady anyway. Her mother takes a small tablet once a day and has never needed insulin in thirty years. Rawan asked whether her own children would get diabetes.

He told her that she has type 1 diabetes and will need insulin for life. He did not consider other types.
h: He told her that she has type 1 diabetes and will need insulin for life

a.o: Dr. Hossam called it type 1 diabetes despite a strong family history, negative antibodies and normal C-peptide.
a.x: Rawan should have had genetic testing for MODY, which might be treated with tablets.
a.w: Diabetes in three generations before 25, no antibodies and preserved insulin suggest MODY. Some types respond to sulfonylureas.

a.o: Dr. Hossam advised carbohydrate counting.
a.x: Counting is not needed.
a.w: Carb counting helps match insulin to food.

a.o: Dr. Hossam adjusted her insulin.
a.x: Insulin should not be changed.
a.w: Adjusting doses is normal care.

a.o: Dr. Hossam praised her control.
a.x: Her HbA1c was too high.
a.w: 53 is near target.

s:
Mrs. Dalia, 40, has Graves' disease. Her eyes have become red, gritty and a bit bulging over three months. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day. Her vision and color vision were normal.

Dr. Rehab checked her eye movements and found mild double vision when looking up. Her thyroid levels were normal on carbimazole.

She prescribed lubricating eye drops and asked the eye clinic to see her.

She works as a hairdresser and said the salon is full of smoke and chemicals. Her eyelids looked puffy, and her eyes were red at the corners. She had trouble closing her eyes fully at night. Her thyroid had been diagnosed eight months ago, and she was on a block-and-replace plan.

She did not mention her smoking, saying "it's not related to the thyroid".
h: She did not mention her smoking, saying "it's not related to the thyroid"

a.o: Dr. Rehab did not tell Mrs. Dalia to stop smoking despite thyroid eye disease.
a.x: She should have been strongly advised and helped to stop smoking.
a.w: Smoking makes thyroid eye disease worse and less responsive to treatment.

a.o: Dr. Rehab prescribed lubricating drops.
a.x: Drops are useless.
a.w: Drops ease gritty, dry eyes.

a.o: Dr. Rehab referred her to the eye clinic.
a.x: The eye clinic is not needed.
a.w: Thyroid eye disease needs an eye specialist.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked her color vision.
a.x: Color vision is irrelevant.
a.w: Losing color vision is a sign of nerve damage.

s:
Hossam, 23, has type 1 diabetes and came in with DKA. After twelve hours of fluids and an insulin infusion, his sugar was 11 mmol/L, his ketones 1.8 and his pH 7.28. He wanted to eat.

Dr. Mai noticed his sugar was now near normal.

She stopped his insulin infusion and his IV fluids and told him to eat breakfast, writing "DKA resolved, sugar normal".

He had come in vomiting and breathing deeply after a night of drinking and missing his insulin. He was now chatty and asked for his phone. His blood pressure was normal and his pulse 88. His chest was clear. His mother was on her way and asked if he could go home today.

She asked him to restart his usual insulin at lunchtime and checked his potassium, which was normal.
h: She stopped his insulin infusion and his IV fluids and told him to eat breakfast, writing "DKA resolved, sugar normal"

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the insulin infusion when Hossam's ketones were still raised, without giving his own insulin first.
a.x: The insulin infusion should have continued, with glucose added, until ketones were below 0.6 and pH normal, and stopped only 30 minutes after his own insulin.
a.w: DKA is resolved when ketones are cleared, not when the sugar is normal. Stopping too early lets DKA come back.

a.o: Dr. Mai let him eat.
a.x: He should stay nil by mouth.
a.w: Eating is fine once he feels well.

a.o: Dr. Mai checked his potassium.
a.x: Potassium was irrelevant.
a.w: Insulin lowers potassium.

a.o: Dr. Mai planned to restart his usual insulin.
a.x: He should stay on the infusion forever.
a.w: Switching back to his usual insulin is the plan.

t: Hypothyroid treated at full dose in heart disease
s:
Mr. Badr, 76, was sent to the clinic because his routine blood test showed a TSH of 38 mU/L and a low free T4. He had felt tired and cold for months, his skin was dry and he had gained weight. His wife said he had become slow and forgetful.

He had a heart attack four years ago and still gets chest tightness when he walks up the hill to the market. He takes aspirin, bisoprolol and a statin. His pulse was 54 and his ECG showed old changes but nothing new.

Dr. Lobna explained that his thyroid gland was underactive and that a daily tablet would replace the missing hormone. She told him to take it in the morning on an empty stomach, half an hour before breakfast, and checked that his wife understood.

Because his levels were so low, she started levothyroxine at the full dose of 125 micrograms a day "to get him better faster". She booked a blood test in six weeks.
h: she started levothyroxine at the full dose of 125 micrograms a day "to get him better faster"

a.o: Dr. Lobna started full-dose levothyroxine in an older man with angina.
a.x: Mr. Badr should have started on a low dose, such as 25 micrograms, and been increased slowly.
a.w: In older people with heart disease, a sudden rise in thyroid hormone makes the heart work harder and can trigger angina or a heart attack.

a.o: Dr. Lobna told him to take the tablet on an empty stomach.
a.x: It should be taken with breakfast.
a.w: Food lowers how much levothyroxine is absorbed.

a.o: Dr. Lobna booked a blood test in six weeks.
a.x: The test should be in a week.
a.w: Thyroid levels take about six weeks to settle after a change.

a.o: Dr. Lobna kept his bisoprolol going.
a.x: Bisoprolol should stop while starting thyroid treatment.
a.w: His bisoprolol protects his heart and should continue.

s:
Mrs. Nahla, 59, has type 2 diabetes on gliclazide. She came to the clinic and, while waiting, felt shaky, sweaty and hungry. The nurse checked her sugar: 3.1 mmol/L. She was awake, talking and able to swallow.

Dr. Yasser saw her at once. He asked when she last ate; she had skipped lunch to get to her appointment on time. She also said she had started walking an hour every afternoon to lose weight, which her daughter had suggested.

He praised her for walking and explained that gliclazide can push the sugar too low when meals are missed. He said they would review her dose.

To treat the low sugar, he gave her two squares of milk chocolate from his drawer and asked her to sit for a while. He said he would recheck her sugar before she drove home.
h: he gave her two squares of milk chocolate from his drawer

a.o: Dr. Yasser treated a low sugar with chocolate.
a.x: Mrs. Nahla should have had a fast sugar like glucose tablets or 150 to 200 mL of juice, then a starchy snack once her sugar was back up.
a.w: The fat in chocolate slows how fast the sugar is absorbed, so it is a poor treatment for a low sugar.

a.o: Dr. Yasser praised her afternoon walks.
a.x: She should stop walking because of the low sugars.
a.w: Walking is good for her diabetes; her medicines may need adjusting instead.

a.o: Dr. Yasser rechecked her sugar before she drove.
a.x: She was fine to drive at once.
a.w: People should not drive until their sugar is safely back up, about 45 minutes after treatment.

a.o: Dr. Yasser said they would review her gliclazide dose.
a.x: The dose was fine.
a.w: Gliclazide often causes low sugars, so a review makes sense.

t: Ibuprofen for a man with an ulcer history
s:
Mr. Amin, 63, came to his GP with a painful, swollen right knee after a week of long walks on a pilgrimage trip. He has had arthritis in both knees for years. He also has high blood pressure, and two years ago he had a bleeding stomach ulcer that was treated with a camera test and acid tablets, which he stopped a year ago because he felt fine.

Dr. Ghada found the knee swollen and stiff but not red or hot to the touch. He had no fever and could put weight on it. His blood pressure was 138/84, and his kidney tests from last month were normal.

She advised ice, a knee support and gentle movement rather than bed rest, and suggested he lose a little weight to take the load off his knees. He laughed and said his wife had been telling him the same for years.

For the pain she prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for two weeks, without anything to protect his stomach, because "the ulcer was years ago". She told him to come back if the knee did not settle.
h: she prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for two weeks, without anything to protect his stomach

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave Mr. Amin ibuprofen with no stomach protection after his bleeding ulcer.
a.x: Mr. Amin should have had paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory gel, or if a tablet NSAID was really needed, a proton pump inhibitor with it.
a.w: A past bleeding ulcer is one of the strongest risks for another bleed on NSAIDs, and the risk does not fade after two years.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Amin to keep moving instead of resting in bed.
a.x: He should have rested the knee completely for two weeks.
a.w: Gentle movement keeps an arthritic knee from stiffening, and bed rest makes it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Amin that losing weight would help his knees.
a.x: Weight has nothing to do with knee pain.
a.w: Every kilo lost takes real load off arthritic knees.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked at Mr. Amin's kidney tests before choosing a painkiller.
a.x: His kidneys had nothing to do with knee pain.
a.w: NSAIDs can harm the kidneys, so recent kidney tests matter before prescribing.

s:
Mr. Sameh, 58, came in after passing black, sticky stools three times since yesterday. He had felt dizzy when he got up to pray this morning. He takes aspirin and clopidogrel after a heart stent eight months ago, and ibuprofen for a bad back.

His pulse was 104 and his blood pressure 102/64. His hemoglobin was 9.6, down from 14 last year, and his urea was raised. Dr. Nada worked out a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 12. A rectal exam showed black stool.

She put in two large drips, sent a blood group and crossmatch and started IV fluids. She stopped his ibuprofen and called the cardiologist about his heart tablets, who advised keeping the aspirin.

He said he felt better after the fluids and wanted to go home to his family. Dr. Nada booked him for an outpatient camera test next week and sent him home with omeprazole tablets, telling him to come back if he felt faint again.
h: Dr. Nada booked him for an outpatient camera test next week and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Sameh home with a high-risk bleed and booked the camera test for next week.
a.x: Mr. Sameh should have been admitted, given an IV proton pump inhibitor after the scope if needed, and had a camera test within 24 hours.
a.w: A Glasgow-Blatchford score of 12 with a fast pulse, low blood pressure and a falling hemoglobin means a high-risk bleed. Only a score of 0 or 1 is safe for home.

a.o: Dr. Nada kept Mr. Sameh's aspirin after talking to the cardiologist.
a.x: All his blood thinners should have stopped at once.
a.w: With a recent stent, stopping all antiplatelets risks a stent clot; cardiology advice to keep aspirin is right.

a.o: Dr. Nada did a rectal exam on Mr. Sameh.
a.x: A rectal exam was pointless.
a.w: Seeing black stool confirms a bleed from high in the gut.

a.o: Dr. Nada stopped Mr. Sameh's ibuprofen.
a.x: Ibuprofen could carry on for his back.
a.w: NSAIDs cause ulcers and bleeding, so stopping them is right.

s:
Mr. Fathi, 58, has liver cirrhosis from hepatitis C. He was admitted with a tight, swollen belly that made it hard to breathe and eat. His legs were swollen too. He had no fever or belly pain, his kidney tests were normal and his sodium was 131.

Dr. Hossam did a small diagnostic tap first, which showed no infection. He then drained 7 liters of fluid from his belly over four hours, and Mr. Fathi said he could breathe properly for the first time in weeks.

He restarted spironolactone and furosemide at a low dose and advised a low-salt diet, not a no-salt one. He asked the dietitian to see him because he had lost muscle in his arms and shoulders, and suggested a late-evening snack.

He did not give any albumin with the large drain, writing "kidneys normal, albumin not needed". He planned to send him home the next day if his blood pressure stayed steady.
h: He did not give any albumin with the large drain

a.o: Dr. Hossam drained 7 liters from Mr. Fathi's belly without giving albumin.
a.x: Mr. Fathi should have had IV albumin, about 8 g for every liter drained.
a.w: Draining more than 5 liters without albumin can cause a drop in blood pressure and kidney failure, even when the kidneys start normal.

a.o: Dr. Hossam did a small tap to check Mr. Fathi's fluid for infection first.
a.x: The test tap was unnecessary with no fever.
a.w: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis can be silent, so every admission with ascites gets a diagnostic tap.

a.o: Dr. Hossam restarted Mr. Fathi's water tablets.
a.x: Diuretics must stop after a large drain.
a.w: Diuretics help stop the fluid from building up again.

a.o: Dr. Hossam suggested a late-evening snack for Mr. Fathi.
a.x: People with cirrhosis should fast at night.
a.w: A bedtime snack reduces muscle breakdown in cirrhosis.

t: Hepatic encephalopathy given a sleeping pill
s:
Mrs. Samira, 62, has cirrhosis. Her son brought her in because she had become muddled over three days. She had been constipated for five days, was sleepy in the day and awake at night, and her hands flapped when she held her arms out. Her sugar and salts were normal.

Dr. Ayman started lactulose to make her open her bowels two or three times a day and added rifaximin. He looked for a trigger: her urine and chest X-ray were clear, and a belly tap showed no infection.

He stopped her nightly antihistamine for itching and asked the nurses to check on her often and keep her safe from falls. Her son was frightened and asked whether she would be herself again; Dr. Ayman said most people improve within days once the bowels move.

At night she was restless and kept pulling at her drip, so Dr. Ayman wrote her up for 10 mg of diazepam "to help her sleep", and asked the nurses to keep the lights low.
h: Dr. Ayman wrote her up for 10 mg of diazepam "to help her sleep"

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave diazepam to calm Mrs. Samira's hepatic encephalopathy.
a.x: Sedatives should have been avoided, with lactulose, calm nursing and family at the bedside to help her settle.
a.w: Benzodiazepines build up in liver failure and deepen the confusion, and can tip her into coma.

a.o: Dr. Ayman stopped Mrs. Samira's antihistamine.
a.x: Her itching tablet should have carried on.
a.w: Sedating antihistamines can worsen encephalopathy.

a.o: Dr. Ayman added rifaximin for Mrs. Samira.
a.x: Rifaximin is only for traveler's diarrhea.
a.w: Rifaximin cuts gut bacteria that make toxins and helps encephalopathy.

a.o: Dr. Ayman aimed for two or three soft motions a day.
a.x: One motion every few days is enough.
a.w: Clearing the bowel removes the toxins that cause confusion.

t: Coeliac test after a gluten-free diet
s:
Reem, 24, came in with bloating, loose stools and tiredness for a year. Her blood tests showed low iron and low folate. Her aunt has coeliac disease. After reading about it online she stopped eating bread and pasta two months ago, and felt a little better.

Dr. Mahmoud examined her belly, which was soft, and checked her weight, which was steady. He asked about her periods, which were light and regular, and about blood in her stool, which she had not seen.

He started iron tablets and sent a coeliac antibody blood test. He told her to carry on with the gluten-free diet while she waited for the result, since it was helping.

Two weeks later the test came back negative. He told her she did not have coeliac disease and could eat what she liked. She asked whether she should still worry about her aunt's illness, and he said no.
h: He told her to carry on with the gluten-free diet while she waited for the result

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud tested Reem for coeliac disease while she was off gluten.
a.x: Reem should have eaten gluten every day for at least six weeks before the blood test.
a.w: Coeliac antibodies fade without gluten, so a negative test on a gluten-free diet means nothing.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Reem about her periods.
a.x: Her periods had nothing to do with her gut.
a.w: Heavy periods are the most common cause of low iron in young women.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud took Reem's aunt's illness seriously.
a.x: Family history doesn't matter in coeliac disease.
a.w: Coeliac disease runs strongly in families.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud started iron tablets while the test was pending.
a.x: Iron should wait until the cause is known.
a.w: Her iron was low and replacing it is safe while tests continue.

t: Acute pancreatitis sent for a scope
s:
Mr. Ramy, 41, came in with severe upper belly pain going through to his back. He had been drinking heavily at his cousin's wedding for two days and had been vomiting all night. His lipase was six times normal.

His pulse was 108 and his blood pressure 120/74. His oxygen was normal. His belly was tender in the upper middle but soft. His liver tests and bilirubin were normal.

Dr. Dina started IV fluids and gave him morphine for the pain, and asked the nurses to measure his urine every hour. A belly ultrasound showed no gallstones and a normal bile duct. She let him sip fluids as soon as the vomiting eased.

She booked him for an urgent ERCP the next morning "to look at the pancreas", and advised him to stop drinking. His brother asked if he would need an operation.
h: She booked him for an urgent ERCP the next morning "to look at the pancreas"

a.o: Dr. Dina booked an ERCP for Mr. Ramy's alcohol pancreatitis with no stones.
a.x: Mr. Ramy should have had fluids, pain relief and early feeding, with no ERCP.
a.w: ERCP is only for pancreatitis with a stone stuck in the bile duct or cholangitis, and it can cause pancreatitis itself.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Mr. Ramy morphine.
a.x: Morphine is banned in pancreatitis.
a.w: Opioids are safe and often needed for pancreatitis pain.

a.o: Dr. Dina let Mr. Ramy start drinking early.
a.x: He should have been nil by mouth for days.
a.w: Early feeding as tolerated helps recovery in pancreatitis.

a.o: Dr. Dina did an ultrasound of Mr. Ramy's gallbladder.
a.x: Ultrasound was pointless since he drinks.
a.w: Gallstones are the other common cause and change the treatment.

t: Red flags missed in an older man with heartburn
s:
Mr. Kamel, 67, came in with heartburn that started three months ago. He had never had it before. He said bread and meat felt like they stuck halfway down his chest, and his belt had needed a new hole because he had lost 6 kg without trying. He smokes and drinks a little.

Dr. Rasha examined him and found nothing abnormal. His blood count showed mild anemia with low iron. He asked whether it could be his new blood pressure tablet, and she checked that it was not a likely cause.

She explained that heartburn is common and gave advice about eating smaller meals, not lying down after eating, raising the head of his bed and stopping smoking.

She prescribed omeprazole for two months and booked a review afterwards to see whether it had worked. She did not refer him for a camera test, writing "trial of PPI first".
h: She did not refer him for a camera test, writing "trial of PPI first"

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mr. Kamel a trial of omeprazole instead of a camera test.
a.x: Mr. Kamel should have been referred urgently for an endoscopy.
a.w: Food sticking, weight loss and anemia are red flags for cancer of the gullet or stomach. They need a scope within two weeks.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Mr. Kamel to raise the head of his bed.
a.x: That trick doesn't help heartburn.
a.w: Raising the bed eases reflux at night.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked whether Mr. Kamel's new tablet was to blame.
a.x: Medicines never cause heartburn.
a.w: Some medicines do worsen reflux, so checking is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Kamel's blood count.
a.x: A blood count was unnecessary.
a.w: The blood count found anemia, another warning sign.

s:
Mrs. Wafaa, 78, was in hospital for a chest infection and had antibiotics for a week. She now had watery diarrhea six times a day, with belly cramps and a fever of 38°C. Her stool test was positive for C. difficile toxin. Her belly was soft and her white count was 13.

Dr. Fouad moved her to a side room and asked staff to wear gloves and aprons and to wash their hands with soap and water, not gel. Her chest course was finished, so he did not start more antibiotics for it, and he stopped her omeprazole.

He started oral vancomycin and gave IV fluids with potassium. He checked her kidney function, which was a little worse, and asked for her fluid intake and stools to be charted.

To ease her diarrhea and let her sleep, he also wrote her up for loperamide after every loose stool. He told her daughter she should be better within a week.
h: he also wrote her up for loperamide after every loose stool

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave Mrs. Wafaa loperamide for C. difficile diarrhea.
a.x: Mrs. Wafaa should not have had anti-diarrhea drugs; vancomycin, fluids and isolation were the right care.
