a.w: Slowing the bowel keeps the toxin in and can cause toxic megacolon, a dangerously swollen colon.

a.o: Dr. Fouad told staff to wash with soap and water, not gel.
a.x: Alcohol gel is enough for any bug.
a.w: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores.

a.o: Dr. Fouad stopped Mrs. Wafaa's omeprazole.
a.x: Her omeprazole should have carried on.
a.w: Acid-lowering drugs raise the risk of C. difficile and its return.

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave oral vancomycin instead of an IV drug.
a.x: IV vancomycin works better.
a.w: IV vancomycin does not reach the bowel; it must be given by mouth.

s:
Mr. Medhat, 52, drinks a bottle of spirits a day and eats very little. He weighs 49 kg. He was admitted with yellow eyes, a swollen belly and shakes. His bilirubin was high and his INR 2.1. His Maddrey score was 48, and a belly tap and blood cultures showed no infection.

Dr. Rehab diagnosed alcoholic hepatitis. She started prednisolone and IV thiamine before any sugar drip, and asked the dietitian to start feeding him through a tube because he could not eat enough.

She told him he must stop drinking completely and asked the addiction team to see him. She started chlordiazepoxide on a careful, shortened plan to prevent alcohol withdrawal.

For a fever of 38.1°C and a headache, she prescribed paracetamol 1 g four times a day. She asked his wife to bring in any medicines from home.
h: she prescribed paracetamol 1 g four times a day

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat full-dose paracetamol.
a.x: Mr. Medhat should have had a reduced dose, for example 500 mg four times a day, no more than 2 g.
a.w: He weighs under 50 kg, drinks heavily and is malnourished with a sick liver, so 4 g a day can harm the liver.

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat thiamine before any sugar.
a.x: Thiamine was not needed.
a.w: Heavy drinkers lack thiamine; sugar first can bring on brain damage.

a.o: Dr. Rehab started chlordiazepoxide in liver disease.
a.x: Benzodiazepines must never be used.
a.w: Withdrawal can cause fits; a careful, short plan is standard.

a.o: Dr. Rehab started prednisolone for Mr. Medhat.
a.x: Steroids are dangerous in liver disease.
a.w: A Maddrey score over 32 with no infection suggests steroids may help.

s:
Mrs. Heba, 28, is 24 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came in with pain on the right side of her belly, higher than her belly button, for a day. It started around her navel. She had felt sick, had no appetite and a temperature of 37.9°C. Her urine test was normal.

Dr. Hamed examined her and found tenderness on the right side just below her ribs. Her white count was 15. The baby's heartbeat was normal on the monitor, and she had no bleeding or tightenings.

He explained that pregnancy stretches the ligaments and that the baby was pushing on her organs. He gave her paracetamol, which helped a little. Her husband asked whether she could eat something before going home.

He sent her home with paracetamol and told her to come back if it got worse. He did not arrange a scan or ask the surgeons to see her.
h: He sent her home with paracetamol and told her to come back if it got worse

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Mrs. Heba home without looking for appendicitis.
a.x: Mrs. Heba should have had an ultrasound or MRI and a surgical review the same day.
a.w: The appendix moves up in pregnancy, so the pain is higher. Fever, nausea and a high white count point to appendicitis, and a burst appendix can cost the baby's life.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked the baby's heartbeat.
a.x: That was unnecessary for belly pain.
a.w: The baby must be checked in any pregnant woman with pain.

a.o: Dr. Hamed gave Mrs. Heba paracetamol.
a.x: Paracetamol is unsafe in pregnancy.
a.w: Paracetamol is safe in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Heba's urine.
a.x: The urine test was pointless.
a.w: A kidney infection can cause similar pain and fever.

t: Crohn's patient told to keep smoking
s:
Ahmed, 26, has Crohn's disease of the last part of his small bowel. He came for review after his second flare this year. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and said smoking was the only thing that helped him relax at work.

Dr. Sherine checked his weight and blood count and arranged a scan of the bowel. She planned to start azathioprine and checked his TPMT enzyme level first, which was normal. She asked for blood tests every week for the first month.

She advised him to have the flu and pneumonia vaccines and to avoid live vaccines once on treatment. She also checked his vitamin B12, which was low, and started injections.

When he asked about smoking, she said he could carry on because "smoking calms bowel inflammation", and booked him back in three months.
h: she said he could carry on because "smoking calms bowel inflammation"

a.o: Dr. Sherine told Ahmed that smoking was fine for his Crohn's disease.
a.x: Ahmed should have been told that smoking makes Crohn's worse and offered help to stop.
a.w: Smoking may ease ulcerative colitis, but it makes Crohn's worse, with more flares and more surgery.

a.o: Dr. Sherine checked Ahmed's TPMT level.
a.x: That test was unnecessary.
a.w: Low TPMT means azathioprine can wipe out the blood count.

a.o: Dr. Sherine checked Ahmed's vitamin B12.
a.x: B12 has nothing to do with Crohn's.
a.w: Crohn's in the last part of the small bowel stops B12 being absorbed.

a.o: Dr. Sherine asked for weekly blood tests.
a.x: Tests were not needed.
a.w: Azathioprine can lower the blood count and harm the liver early on.

t: IBS label in an older woman
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 61, came in with bloating almost every day for three months. She also felt full after a few mouthfuls, had lost her appetite, and needed to pass urine more often. She had no diarrhea. She had never had bowel problems before.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found a soft belly that looked slightly swollen. Her blood count and kidney tests were normal. She said her friend had IBS and had been helped by peppermint oil.

He told her she had irritable bowel syndrome, which is common and not dangerous. He advised a low FODMAP diet and peppermint oil capsules, and told her stress could make it worse.

He booked a review in three months to see whether the diet had helped, and did not arrange any other tests. She was relieved and thanked him.
h: He told her she had irritable bowel syndrome, which is common and not dangerous

a.o: Dr. Ihab diagnosed IBS in Mrs. Fawzia, who is over 60 with new bloating.
a.x: Mrs. Fawzia should have had a CA125 blood test and a pelvic ultrasound to look for ovarian cancer.
a.w: New, constant bloating and early fullness in a woman over 50 can be ovarian cancer. IBS rarely starts after 50.

a.o: Dr. Ihab suggested peppermint oil capsules.
a.x: Peppermint oil is useless.
a.w: Peppermint oil can ease IBS-type cramps and bloating.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Fawzia's blood count.
a.x: Blood tests were not needed.
a.w: Blood tests help look for other causes.

a.o: Dr. Ihab mentioned that stress can make bowel symptoms worse.
a.x: That was unkind and untrue.
a.w: Stress does worsen gut symptoms in many people.

s:
Mr. Saad, 60, has cirrhosis with fluid in his belly. His wife brought him in because he had become slow and muddled over two days. He had a temperature of 37.9°C. His belly was swollen but only mildly tender, and his creatinine had risen from 90 to 150.

Dr. Mona checked his urine and chest X-ray, both clear, and sent blood cultures. She started lactulose for the confusion and stopped his water tablets because of his kidneys.

She thought the fever was from a virus going round the family. She did not tap his belly fluid, writing "no peritonitis signs, only mildly tender".

She gave him paracetamol 500 mg for the fever and asked the nurses to watch his urine output. She planned to see him again on the morning round.
h: She did not tap his belly fluid

a.o: Dr. Mona skipped a tap of Mr. Saad's belly fluid.
a.x: Mr. Saad should have had a diagnostic tap at once and IV antibiotics plus albumin if the white cells were high.
a.w: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis often has few belly signs. With fever, confusion and worse kidneys in cirrhosis it is common and deadly if missed.

a.o: Dr. Mona stopped Mr. Saad's water tablets.
a.x: The diuretics should have carried on.
a.w: Diuretics worsen kidney injury and must stop when kidneys fail.

a.o: Dr. Mona sent blood cultures from Mr. Saad.
a.x: Cultures were pointless.
a.w: Blood cultures help find the infection and guide antibiotics.

a.o: Dr. Mona gave Mr. Saad paracetamol.
a.x: Paracetamol is banned in liver disease.
a.w: Small doses of paracetamol are the safest painkiller in cirrhosis.

s:
Mrs. Nadia, 46, was admitted with mild pancreatitis caused by gallstones. An ultrasound showed stones in her gallbladder and a normal bile duct. She improved over four days with fluids, pain relief and early eating. Her blood tests were back to normal.

Dr. Waleed explained that a small stone had passed through and irritated the pancreas. He checked that she was eating a normal meal without pain and stopped her drip.

He advised her to cut down on fatty food while she waited, and prescribed paracetamol. He did not book an ERCP, as her bile duct and liver tests were normal.

He discharged her and told her the surgeons would see her in clinic in three months to discuss removing her gallbladder. Her husband asked whether it could happen again.
h: told her the surgeons would see her in clinic in three months to discuss removing her gallbladder

a.o: Dr. Waleed left Mrs. Nadia's gallbladder surgery for three months.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia should have had her gallbladder removed during this admission or within two weeks.
a.w: After mild gallstone pancreatitis, the risk of another attack is high while waiting, and some attacks are severe.

a.o: Dr. Waleed decided Mrs. Nadia didn't need an ERCP.
a.x: Every gallstone pancreatitis needs an ERCP.
a.w: ERCP is only for a blocked duct or cholangitis; her duct and liver tests were normal.

a.o: Dr. Waleed told Mrs. Nadia to cut down on fatty food.
a.x: Food has nothing to do with gallstones.
a.w: Fatty meals can bring on gallstone pain while waiting.

a.o: Dr. Waleed let Mrs. Nadia eat early.
a.x: She should have fasted until discharge.
a.w: Early eating is safe and helps in mild pancreatitis.

s:
Mr. Hany, 62, came in for a blood pressure check. At the end he mentioned dark red blood mixed in with his stool a few times over the last month, and that he had been more tired than usual. His father had bowel cancer at 70.

Dr. Abeer checked his blood pressure, which was well controlled, and renewed his tablets. A blood count she had taken last week showed anemia with low iron. He had no belly pain and his weight was steady.

She said the blood was probably from piles because he had been constipated, gave him a soothing cream and advised more fiber and water. She gave him iron tablets for the anemia.

She did not examine his back passage or refer him, writing "likely hemorrhoids", and booked a review in three months.
h: She did not examine his back passage or refer him, writing "likely hemorrhoids"

a.o: Dr. Abeer blamed piles for Mr. Hany's bleeding with anemia.
a.x: Mr. Hany should have had a rectal exam and an urgent referral for a colonoscopy.
a.w: Rectal bleeding with iron-deficiency anemia over 60, and a father with bowel cancer, can be bowel cancer.

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mr. Hany iron tablets.
a.x: Iron should wait until the cause is found.
a.w: Iron can start while tests are arranged.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked about Mr. Hany's father.
a.x: Family history doesn't matter.
a.w: Bowel cancer in a parent raises his risk.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised more fiber and water.
a.x: Fiber makes bleeding worse.
a.w: Fiber eases constipation and straining.

s:
Mr. Hassan, 55, has lymphoma and is due to start chemotherapy with rituximab. His screening blood tests showed he had hepatitis B in the past: core antibody positive, surface antigen negative. His liver tests were normal. He remembered being yellow as a young man in the army.

Dr. Nermine explained the treatment and its side effects. She checked his HIV and hepatitis C tests, which were negative, and asked for a heart scan before the chemotherapy.

She told him to avoid people with chickenpox and to call the ward at once if he had a fever. She gave him written information for his family.

She said that because his surface antigen was negative, the hepatitis B had cleared and nothing else was needed. She did not start an antiviral medicine.
h: She did not start an antiviral medicine

a.o: Dr. Nermine gave Mr. Hassan rituximab with no hepatitis B protection.
a.x: Mr. Hassan should have had an antiviral such as entecavir during rituximab and for at least a year after.
a.w: Rituximab can wake up hidden hepatitis B, even with a negative surface antigen, and cause liver failure.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked Mr. Hassan for HIV and hepatitis C.
a.x: That screening was unnecessary.
a.w: Hidden viral infections must be found before chemotherapy.

a.o: Dr. Nermine asked for a heart scan.
a.x: His heart had nothing to do with lymphoma.
a.w: Some lymphoma drugs can harm the heart.

a.o: Dr. Nermine told Mr. Hassan to call with any fever.
a.x: A fever can wait for clinic.
a.w: Fever on chemotherapy can be life-threatening sepsis.

t: Constipation in a child given an enema
s:
Laila, 5, came in with her mother because of belly pain and hard, large stools every five days for three months. She cries on the toilet and hides to hold it in. Her belly was soft with a firm stool mass on the left side. She was growing normally and had no vomiting.

Dr. Rana asked about her diet, which had little fruit or vegetables, and about her back and legs, which were normal. She checked the skin over her lower back for any dimple, and there was none.

She explained that Laila had constipation and that holding in stool makes it harder and more painful. She advised more water and fruit and a reward chart for sitting on the toilet after meals.

She gave Laila a phosphate enema in the ER and sent her home with no medicine, saying "the enema will fix it".
h: She gave Laila a phosphate enema in the ER and sent her home with no medicine

a.o: Dr. Rana treated Laila's long-term constipation with only an enema.
a.x: Laila should have had oral macrogol to clear the stool and then keep it soft for months.
a.w: Enemas frighten children and don't stop the cycle. Macrogol by mouth for months is first-line.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Laila's lower back.
a.x: That was unnecessary in constipation.
a.w: A spinal problem can cause constipation, so checking the back is good practice.

a.o: Dr. Rana suggested a reward chart.
a.x: Charts are childish and useless.
a.w: Toilet routines and rewards help children with constipation.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked about Laila's diet.
a.x: Diet doesn't matter.
a.w: A diet low in fiber can cause constipation.

s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 34, was admitted three days ago after taking a large paracetamol overdose. She has been on acetylcysteine since she arrived. Today her INR has risen from 2.5 to 4.8, her pH is 7.24 and her creatinine 260. She has become more confused.

Dr. Ahmed continued the acetylcysteine and gave IV fluids. He checked her sugar every hour because it had been low, and started a glucose drip.

He asked the psychiatrists to see her when she was well enough. He spoke honestly to her family, telling them she was very ill.

He decided to wait until the next morning to call the liver transplant center, "to see if she improves overnight".
h: He decided to wait until the next morning to call the liver transplant center

a.o: Dr. Ahmed waited until morning to call the liver unit for Mrs. Asmaa.
a.x: Mrs. Asmaa should have been discussed with the liver transplant center at once.
a.w: A pH below 7.3 after paracetamol, with a rising INR and confusion, meets transplant criteria. Hours matter.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed kept acetylcysteine going.
a.x: It should stop after the usual course.
a.w: Acetylcysteine continues while the liver is failing.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed checked Mrs. Asmaa's sugar every hour.
a.x: Sugar checks were unnecessary.
a.w: A failing liver cannot make sugar, so low sugar is common.

a.o: Dr. Ahmed told the family she was very ill.
a.x: That was too frightening.
a.w: Families need honest information.

s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 39, had burning upper belly pain for three months, worse at night. He had no weight loss, no trouble swallowing and no black stools. He started omeprazole from the pharmacy a week ago, which helped.

Dr. Ghada thought he might have the stomach bug H. pylori. She asked about painkillers, and he said he took no ibuprofen or aspirin. She sent a stool test for the bacterium that same day.

The test came back negative, so she told him he did not have H. pylori. She did not refer him for a camera test, as he was young with no warning signs.

She advised him to keep taking omeprazole for a month and to cut down on coffee and late meals. He asked whether his brother, who had an ulcer, should be tested too.
h: She sent a stool test for the bacterium that same day

a.o: Dr. Ghada tested Mr. Ibrahim for H. pylori while he was on omeprazole.
a.x: He should have stopped omeprazole for two weeks before the test.
a.w: Proton pump inhibitors can make H. pylori tests falsely negative.

a.o: Dr. Ghada did not send Mr. Ibrahim for a camera test.
a.x: Everyone with stomach pain needs a scope.
a.w: Young people with no warning signs can be tested and treated without a scope.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Ibrahim about painkillers.
a.x: Painkillers were off topic.
a.w: NSAIDs are a common cause of ulcers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised cutting down on late meals.
a.x: Meal timing doesn't matter.
a.w: Late meals can worsen night-time symptoms.

s:
Mr. Sami, 45, has hepatitis C with early liver scarring and is on tablets that should cure it. He came to clinic before a three-month work trip to a country where hepatitis A is common. He was excited about the job and asked what he should watch for.

Dr. Nadia checked his liver blood tests, which were stable, and asked about alcohol; he drinks very little. She checked that he had enough tablets for the trip and gave him a letter for airport security.

She checked his hepatitis B blood test, which showed he was already immune from a vaccine years ago, and told him so.

She gave him advice about clean food and bottled water. She did not offer a hepatitis A vaccine, saying "you already have hepatitis".
h: She did not offer a hepatitis A vaccine, saying "you already have hepatitis"

a.o: Dr. Nadia didn't offer Mr. Sami a hepatitis A vaccine.
a.x: Mr. Sami should have been vaccinated against hepatitis A before his trip.
a.w: Hepatitis A on top of liver disease can cause liver failure. Having one hepatitis virus doesn't protect against another.

a.o: Dr. Nadia checked Mr. Sami's hepatitis B immunity.
a.x: That test was off topic.
a.w: If he were not immune, he would need a hepatitis B vaccine too.

a.o: Dr. Nadia gave Mr. Sami a letter for his tablets.
a.x: A letter was unnecessary.
a.w: Carrying a letter avoids trouble with medicines at airports.

a.o: Dr. Nadia asked Mr. Sami about alcohol.
a.x: Alcohol was irrelevant.
a.w: Alcohol speeds liver damage in hepatitis C.

s:
Mrs. Rana, 33, has ulcerative colitis. She was admitted with bloody diarrhea ten times a day, a pulse of 104 and a temperature of 37.9°C. Her CRP was high and her albumin low. An X-ray of her belly showed no swelling of the colon.

Dr. Hossam started IV hydrocortisone and a daily blood thinner injection to prevent clots. He sent stool tests for infection, including C. difficile.

He asked the surgeons to see her on the first day in case she did not improve, and planned to review her on day three to decide on rescue treatment.

To slow the diarrhea and help her sleep, he also gave her loperamide and codeine. Her mother was worried about the blood thinner and asked if it would make the bleeding worse.
h: To slow the diarrhea and help her sleep, he also gave her loperamide and codeine

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave Mrs. Rana loperamide and codeine in a severe colitis flare.
a.x: Mrs. Rana should not have had anti-diarrhea drugs or opioids.
a.w: In severe colitis these drugs can cause toxic megacolon, where the colon swells and can burst.

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave Mrs. Rana a blood thinner while she was bleeding.
a.x: Blood thinners are dangerous with bloody diarrhea.
a.w: Severe colitis raises clot risk, and preventive blood thinners are standard.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked the surgeons to see her on day one.
a.x: Surgeons should only come if she gets worse.
a.w: Early surgical review is advised in severe colitis.

a.o: Dr. Hossam tested Mrs. Rana's stool for C. difficile.
a.x: Tests were unnecessary in a known colitis patient.
a.w: Infection can mimic or worsen a flare.

s:
Mr. Atef, 59, has cirrhosis and was admitted vomiting blood. His blood pressure was 92/60 and his hemoglobin 7.2. He was given blood to bring his hemoglobin up to about 8, and terlipressin. A camera test showed bleeding varices, which were banded.

Dr. Mai wrote him up for lactulose because blood in the gut can bring on confusion. She held his propranolol while his blood pressure was low.

She asked for him to be watched closely for more bleeding, with the camera team ready to repeat the scope. She spoke to his son, who asked if his father would bleed again.

She did not start any antibiotics, writing "no signs of infection, no fever".
h: She did not start any antibiotics, writing "no signs of infection, no fever"

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mr. Atef no antibiotics after his variceal bleed.
a.x: Mr. Atef should have had IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone from admission.
a.w: In cirrhosis with a gut bleed, antibiotics lower infection, rebleeding and death, even without fever.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped the blood at a hemoglobin of about 8.
a.x: She should have given blood until it was normal.
a.w: Overfilling raises the pressure in the varices and causes rebleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mai held Mr. Atef's propranolol.
a.x: His beta blocker should have carried on.
a.w: Beta blockers are paused while the blood pressure is low from bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mai gave Mr. Atef lactulose.
a.x: Lactulose was not needed.
a.w: Blood in the gut can trigger encephalopathy.

s:
Mr. Sabri, 70, had an operation on his bowel two years ago. He came in with cramping belly pain, green vomiting and no stool or wind for two days. His belly was swollen and his bowel sounds were high-pitched and tinkling. His hernia sites were normal.

Dr. Inas sent bloods, which showed he was dry, and started a drip. She did an X-ray, which showed dilated loops of small bowel in the middle of the belly.

She asked about his medicines: he takes codeine for his back. She gave him an anti-sickness injection and checked his potassium, which was low, and added it to the drip.

She diagnosed constipation from codeine, gave him a strong laxative to drink, and asked the nurses to let him eat and drink normally.
h: She diagnosed constipation from codeine, gave him a strong laxative to drink

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Sabri laxatives for small bowel obstruction.
a.x: Mr. Sabri should have been nil by mouth, with a drip, a nasogastric tube, a CT scan and a surgical review.
a.w: Vomiting, no wind, a swollen belly and dilated loops after old surgery mean adhesions blocking the bowel. Laxatives can make it burst.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Mr. Sabri's hernia sites.
a.x: That was unnecessary.
a.w: A trapped hernia is a common cause of obstruction.

a.o: Dr. Inas replaced Mr. Sabri's potassium.
a.x: Potassium was off topic.
a.w: Low potassium slows the bowel and needs replacing.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked about Mr. Sabri's codeine.
a.x: His medicines had nothing to do with it.
a.w: Codeine causes constipation and is worth knowing.

s:
It was almost five in the afternoon when Mr. Tarek rushed into the ER carrying his nephew Omar, a skinny nine-year-old with a towel pressed to his left arm. Omar had crashed his bicycle into broken glass outside the bakery. By the time they arrived the bleeding had stopped, but the towel was soaked and Omar was pale and crying.

Nurse Salma checked him quickly. His heart was racing at 112, but his blood pressure was fine and he was talking clearly, so she put him in the yellow area. Omar weighed 28 kg, had no allergies his uncle knew of, and had his last tetanus shot at six.

Dr. Hany unwrapped the towel and found a clean 5 cm cut on the inside of the forearm. Omar could move every finger. "We'll need stitches," Dr. Hany said. Mr. Tarek nodded. "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him." Dr. Hany washed the wound, numbed it with lidocaine and closed it with six neat stitches. He gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol for the pain and sent him home with his uncle and a wound-care leaflet.
h: "His parents are at work, but go ahead, I'm responsible for him."

a.o: Dr. Hany stitched Omar's arm after only his uncle agreed, when his parents were a phone call away.
a.x: Dr. Hany should have phoned Omar's parents for consent before stitching.
a.w: An uncle is not Omar's legal guardian. The bleeding had stopped, so this was not an emergency and there was time to reach a parent.

a.o: Nurse Salma sent Omar to the yellow area, when a child cut by glass with a racing heart should be seen first.
a.x: Omar should have gone straight to the red area.
a.w: Yellow was right: the bleeding had stopped, his blood pressure was normal and he was talking. A fast heart in a scared, crying child is not shock.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Omar 420 mg of paracetamol, far too much for a 28 kg boy.
a.x: Omar should have had 280 mg of paracetamol.
a.w: 420 mg is 15 mg/kg for a 28 kg child, a normal dose.

a.o: Omar went home without a tetanus shot after falling on dirty glass.
a.x: Omar should have had a tetanus booster before leaving.
a.w: His last tetanus shot was three years ago. A dirty wound needs a booster only if the last one was more than 5 years ago.
